notes:
I ran out of search and fetch tools before I'd covered the whole psalm. Verses 1–22 are well covered. Verses 23–35 depend mostly on a short overview (Bridgeway, Donald Flemming) and a few notes on vv. 30–31. I found nothing from Lutheran sites, Orthodox sites, the NET Bible notes or Bible Odyssey, and no prosperity, word‑of‑faith or hyper‑grace teaching on this psalm. Augustine (Catholic) is covered only for vv. 1–7.

**Introduction**
- Most commentators link the psalm to the ark being brought into Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). The Anglican Church assigned it to Pentecost ("Whitsunday") because of the gifts given at the ascension in v. 18, which Ephesians 4 quotes. Adam Clarke called it the hardest psalm in the Psalter. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-68/
- Gaebelein notes that God is named in seven different forms in this psalm. https://studylight.org/commentaries/gab/psalms-68.html

**v. 1:**
- Using the phrasing of Numbers 10:35, David proclaimed the triumph of God over all His enemies. Guzik adds that the verse also fits Christ's resurrection: when Jesus rose, His enemies scattered. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-68/
- Pulpit says both this verse and Numbers 10:35 express confidence that God's enemies scatter whenever He arises; neither refers to any one special occasion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Benson points out a grammar difference. The Hebrew in Numbers is a command ("Let God arise"), while here it is future: God shall, or will, arise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/68-1.htm
- Spurgeon says the words picture the Lord holding back for a while and letting His enemies rage, and that we too may plead with Him to act. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-68.html
- Catholic (Augustine): he applies the vanishing smoke to those who shouted "Crucify" and were then defeated by the very One they mocked. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801068.htm

**v. 2:**
- Pulpit: the wicked vanish as smoke does in wind and as wax melts in a hot fire. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Guzik contrasts this with Ephesians 6, where believers *stand* in spiritual battle. Here God's enemies cannot stand at all. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-68/
- Augustine reads it two ways: hard hearts melting in repentance, or a warning of final judgment. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801068.htm

**v. 3:**
- Pulpit: when the wicked are destroyed, the righteous are relieved and rejoice at God's goodness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Augustine connects their joy to Christ's words, Come, you blessed of My Father, receive ye the kingdom. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801068.htm

**v. 4:**
- Guzik, quoting VanGemeren: "rides on the clouds" sets Israel's God against Baal, whom the Canaanites called "the Rider on the clouds." Spurgeon calls "Jah" a concentrated, not lesser, form of God's name. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-68/
- Translation question: Pulpit notes the line is now generally rendered "Cast up a highway for him that rideth through the deserts," picturing a road prepared for a travelling king (compare Isaiah 40:3). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) links the name Yah to the Hebrew name of Jesus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html

**v. 5:**
- Guzik: God's greatness shows in caring for the weak as well as in winning battles. Boice says earthly kings surround themselves with the powerful, but God surrounds Himself with the miserable. Bonar links the verse to James 1:27. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-68/
- Pulpit takes "holy habitation" to mean God's heavenly dwelling rather than the tabernacle or temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm

**v. 6:**
- Pulpit: "solitary" means outcasts and wanderers given a home, chiefly nomadic Israel settled in Canaan. The Exodus is in view but not exclusively, since God also frees people from their own sins. The rebellious are left in the "dry land" of their own stubbornness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Guzik applies "families" to lonely people today, who should seek out such relationships. He notes that "into prosperity" is not a blessing promised to the rebellious. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-68/
- Augustine reads the line as God making people of one mind live together in one house, which he calls the Lord's holy place. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801068.htm

**vv. 7–8:**
- Pulpit: these verses echo the Song of Deborah (Judges 5:4–5) and the thunderstorm at Sinai (Exodus 19). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Spurgeon (via Guzik): the wilderness "wanderings" were a planned march, not aimless straying. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-68/
- Augustine: God's "going forth" is seen in His works, but only by those who know how to look for them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801068.htm

**vv. 9–10:**
- Pulpit: the "rain" is a shower of blessings (manna, quail, water, victories), not literal rain. "The poor" are Israel, worn down in Egypt and the wilderness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Poole (via Guzik) allows either the wilderness or the land of Canaan. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-68/

**v. 11 — the Protestant traditions differ here:**
- Pulpit: literally, a great company of women heralded the word. This recalls women's victory choirs (Miriam, Deborah, the women who greeted David). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Gill (Baptist) reads it of the apostles, the seventy and later preachers, as an "army" of ministers. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nas/psalms/68-11.html
- Guzik (Calvary Chapel) links the verse to women being the first witnesses of the resurrection. He adds that women should not hold positions of doctrinal authority (1 Timothy 2), though they can and should proclaim the gospel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-68/
- A Bible Hub article argues the opposite: restricting proclamation to men would contradict the explicit language of the text. https://biblehub.com/q/Psalm_68_11_Women_s_role_in_God_s_word.htm

**vv. 12–13:**
- Guzik: kings flee, and even those who stayed home share the spoil. He calls this the gospel picture: we gain from a battle Christ fought. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-68/
- Pulpit reads v. 13 differently, as a rebuke to tribes who stayed home among the sheepfolds (as in Judges 5:16). In this reading the silver and gold dove describes their comfort, not a promise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Kidner (via Guzik) lists several readings of the dove and suggests the women showing off their new finery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-68/

**v. 14:**
- Pulpit: the Hebrew only says "it snows on Salmon," so something may be missing. Cheyne pictures the ground covered with glittering abandoned armour. Salmon was a wooded hill near Shechem. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Guzik says the meaning is not clear. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-68/

**vv. 15–16:**
- Pulpit: Bashan is a huge "mountain of God," yet the lower Zion was chosen. The peaks "look askance" in jealousy, and Zion is God's permanent home, unlike Sinai. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Chuck Smith makes the same point about the jealous hills. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html

**v. 17:**
- Pulpit: God moves from Sinai to Zion with a host of angels, and the glory of Sinai is in effect transferred to the sanctuary. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm

**v. 18 — the traditions differ on how this points to Christ:**
- The original setting (Pulpit): God went up with the ark to Zion, took captives and received tribute from Israel's enemies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Got Questions on Paul's change from "received" to "gave" gifts: conquering kings received tribute and then shared it with their people. Its point is that Christ is a conquering king who gives gifts to His people. https://www.gotquestions.org/captives-in-your-train.html
- Constable suggests Paul may have followed the Targum, which applied the verse to Moses giving gifts to men. Gill likewise notes that the Targum, Syriac and Arabic versions say "gave." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html and https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/ephesians/4-8.html
- Methodist (Wesley): the verse refers plainly to Christ's ascension, in whom alone it is literally accomplished. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html
- Reformed (Calvin): the first meaning is David's reign replacing Saul's. David foreshadowed Christ, whose "descent" was His humiliation and death. "Received" and "gave" mean the same thing, because Christ shares the spoils with His church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html
- Barnes (Presbyterian): the verse did not originally refer to Christ. Paul borrowed language that fits Christ's triumph. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html
- Calvary Chapel (Chuck Smith): before the cross, Hades had two compartments, and at His death Christ freed the Old Testament faithful and led them up. The "gifts" are apostles, prophets, evangelists and pastor‑teachers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html
- Gaebelein also says the Redeemer first descended into death and the grave. https://studylight.org/commentaries/gab/psalms-68.html

**v. 19:**
- Pulpit gives the better rendering as "day by day he will bear our burden," not the KJV's "loadeth us with benefits." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Chuck Smith, using the KJV wording, rejoices in the daily benefits of serving Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html

**v. 20:**
- Pulpit: God is a God of saving deeds, and escape from death comes only through Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Chuck Smith: our times are in God's hands. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html

**v. 21:**
- Pulpit: God gives escape from death, but He will still strike His enemies fatally. Kay thinks the "hairy scalp" points to Absalom; others see the young and strong. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm

**vv. 22–23:**
- Pulpit: the KJV's added words "my people" are a mistake. God is threatening His enemies: even if they hide in Bashan or the sea, He will bring them back for judgment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Bridgeway: nothing from Bashan to the sea can withstand God, and Israel will triumph. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html

**vv. 24–27:**
- Bridgeway: singers, musicians, dancers and tribal leaders enter the sanctuary in a triumphal procession. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html
- Chuck Smith describes the order of the procession and argues for more variety in worship than rows of pews. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html

**vv. 28–31:**
- Bridgeway: other nations will no longer tax Israel but bring offerings as they submit to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html
- v. 30: the "beast in the reeds" is usually taken as Egypt, pictured as a crocodile or hippopotamus by the Nile (Ellicott; Horne via Benson). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/68-30.htm
- Spurgeon's notes include one view that the "bulls" and "calves" are Egypt's animal gods. They also mention a view that a lion is meant. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps068.cfm
- v. 31: Cush is the region of modern Sudan and Ethiopia. Bible Hub sees the Ethiopian official of Acts 8 as an early fulfilment. https://biblehub.com/psalms/68-31.htm

**vv. 32–35:**
- Bridgeway: all nations are called to praise the One who rules in the heavens. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/68-18.html

**Modern scholarship (only what the sites I read report):**
- The Baal "rider on the clouds" background (v. 4): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-68/
- Possible fragments of older poems and a gap in the text at v. 14: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/68.htm
- Grätz suggested changing a word in v. 30, and one clause there still has no satisfying explanation: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/68-30.htm
- MacLaren says scholars who date the psalm to David and those who date it after the exile both claim the Egypt reference supports them: https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/the-expositors-bible/psalms-volume-two/psalm-sixty-eight.cfm
